title: Ovid: Change as Story
subtitle: A Roman poem opens with transformation

learningObjectives.text: What subject does Ovid announce in the proem?
What does Daphne become in Ovid's Book I episode?

proem.author: Ovid
proem.locator: Book I · Proem [I.1-4]; Book I · Proem [I.1-4], normalized characters 0-235
proem.excerpt: My design leads me to speak of forms changed into new bodies.[1] Ye Gods, (for you it was who changed them,) favor my attempts,[2] and bring down the lengthened narrative from the very beginning of the world, {even} to my own times.[3]
proem.note: Verbatim translated verse from Ovid. Riley's arguments, synopses, notes, and explanations are separately indexed and are not quoted as primary verse.

daphne.author: Ovid
daphne.locator: Book I · Fable XII [I.452-567]; Book I · Fable XII [I.452-567], normalized characters 6392-7086
daphne.excerpt: Her strength being {now} spent, she grows pale, and being quite faint, with the fatigue of so swift a flight, looking upon the waters of Peneus, she says, “Give me, my father, thy aid, if you rivers have divine power. Oh Earth, either yawn {to swallow me}, or by changing it, destroy that form, by which I have pleased too much, and which causes me to be injured.” Hardly had she ended her prayer, {when} a heavy torpor seizes her limbs; {and} her soft breasts are covered with a thin bark. Her hair grows into green leaves, her arms into branches; her feet, the moment before so swift, adhere by sluggish roots; a {leafy} canopy overspreads her features; her elegance alone[84] remains in her.
daphne.note: Verbatim translated verse from Ovid. Riley's arguments, synopses, notes, and explanations are separately indexed and are not quoted as primary verse.

narrativeBlocks.title: The poem's opening promise
narrativeBlocks.body: Ovid's proem announces a poem about forms changed into new bodies, extending from the world's beginning to his own time.

narrativeBlocks.title: The transformation theme
narrativeBlocks.body: Source quotation (Riley's translation; whitespace normalized): “My design leads me to speak of forms changed into new bodies.[1] Ye Gods, (for you it was who changed them,) favor my attempts,[2] and bring down the lengthened narrative from the very beginning of the world, {even} to my own times.[3]”

narrativeBlocks.title: Daphne becomes a laurel
narrativeBlocks.body: In Book I, Daphne flees Apollo and calls for help. Her body changes into a tree; Apollo addresses the laurel as the tree he will wear.

narrativeBlocks.title: Roman literary reception
narrativeBlocks.body: This is Ovid's Roman epic in Henry T. Riley's nineteenth-century English translation, not neutral evidence for every Greek version or Roman cult practice.

narrativeBlocks.title: Follow the change in the scene
narrativeBlocks.body: The proem's promise becomes a concrete episode: pursuit ends in bodily transformation, while Apollo gives the laurel a continuing role in his own story.
